items.text: A boat is at sea. It travels from China to San Francisco. It is going fast. It takes part in a competition . A man is on the boat. He is working. An accident happens. Wind moves the man. He falls into the water. The water is very cold. The man is not safe. His friends look for him. They must find him. They find him in one and a half hour. The man is in shock. He is very cold. Difficult words: take part (do something), competition (situation when people try to be better than others). You can read the original story and watch the video in the Level 3 section.

An accident happened during the World Clipper Race, where competitors currently race to San Francisco from China. A competitor was changing a sail when he fell over the side of his boat. The high winds swept him away from the ship. He fell into the ice-cold water. People on the ship looked for him. It took them about one and a half hour long. The man was in shock and his body temperature was very low. Difficult words: clipper (fast ship), sail (large piece of strong cloth fixed onto a boat), sweep (move or push). You can read the original story and watch the video in the Level 3 section.

“Mayday! Mayday! Mayday! We have a man overboard.” These chilling cries for help were called out in the early hours of Monday morning, as a British man was rescued from the Pacific Ocean, after falling overboard during the World Clipper Race. Andrew Taylor, from London, was changing a sail with a fellow crew member when he went over the side and was dunked into the ice-cold water. After being swept away from the yacht by high winds, he spent about one and a half hours in the Pacific before he was plucked from the ocean by his team-mates. Speaking back on board the boat Andrew, who is being treated for shock and hypothermia, said he feared the crew would not be able to find him. “I didn’t know if you were looking for me or not. I didn’t know if you’d see me.” “Didn’t you hear Shane shout?” “No, I heard nothing. And then I saw somebody at the mast . Initially , I thought it was a good thing because I knew you were looking for me, and then I realised that it might be a bad thing because it meant you didn’t know where I was.” The terrifying incident happened during race 10 in the 16th stage of the Round the World Race, currently racing to San Francisco from Qingdao in China. Difficult words: clipper (fast sailing ship), sail (large piece of strong cloth fixed onto a boat), dunk (fall into the water), pluck (pick up), mast (tall upright piece of wood which carries a sail), initially (in the beginning). Source: www.itn.co.uk

An earthquake hits in Chile. It happens in the north of the country. One woman says that the earthquake is strong. Everything moves. The earthquake lasts a long time, too. The earthquake makes a tsunami . People run away. They run to the mountains. Prisoners use the situation. They escape from jail. The police catch 16 of the prisoners. The police look for the rest of them. Difficult words: earthquake (when the ground moves), tsunami (very big wave), prisoner (person who is in jail). You can read the original story and watch the video in the Level 3 section.

An earthquake struck off the coast of Chile. The quake hit near the Peruvian border. A woman said that the earthquake was strong and that everything in the old part of the city moved a lot. Another woman said that the earthquake lasted a long time. She said that all she and others could do was pray with their daughter. The earthquake triggered a tsunami. The government evacuated thousands of people from low-lying areas. Prisoners took advantage of the situation and escaped from jail. The police recaptured about 16 of the female prisoners, but security forces are still in search of the rest. Difficult words: trigger (start), take advantage (use a situation to do something you want), low-lying (place that is not high above the water), recapture (catch). You can read the original story and watch the video in the Level 3 section.

A major earthquake has struck off the coast of Chile. The 8.2 magnitude quake hit around 100 kilometres northwest of Iquique near the Peruvian border. It triggered a tsunami with the biggest wave reported at just over two metres. At least five people have died. This woman said it was too strong and that everything in the old part of the city moved a lot. While this resident said it was very long and all they could do was pray with their daughter. There was an evacuation from the low-lying city up the mountainside and authorities said thousands of people had been on the move. The tsunami warning had been in place until early this morning. The area around Iquique has been on alert in recent weeks due to a number of tremors . It is a key copper exporting port, but firms said there had been no serious damage to the operations. Prisoners took advantage of the confusion and escaped jail. Some 16 of the women were recaptured, but security forces have been searching for the rest. Difficult words: trigger (start), tremor (small earthquake). Source: www.itn.co.uk

There is a show in a museum in New York. It is about pterosaurs. Pterosaurs live 66 million years ago. These animals can fly. However, they are not related to birds. They are related to dinosaurs. They are a unique group of animals. They are the biggest flying animals. Their wings are really big. One wing is around 5 metres long. The animals have a backbone and they can fly. This makes them really special. Difficult words: related to (like), wing (part of the body which makes the animal fly), backbone (line of bones in your back). You can read the original story and watch the video in the Level 3 section.

There is a new exhibition at a New York museum. It is about pterosaurs. Pterosaurs were not related to bats, nor to birds. They were closely related to dinosaurs, but they were not dinosaurs. They were a unique group. These animals lived 66 million years ago. They were the first animals with backbones to evolve powered flight. They were really unique in that way. They were also the largest flying animals we know of right now. Some of the pterosaurs had wing spans up to ten meters across! Difficult words: backbone (row of bones down the centre of your back), evolve (change their bodies over time to be able to fly), wing span (size of the wings). You can read the original story and watch the video in the Level 3 section.

The largest flying vertebrates in earth’s history are taking to the air at The American Museum of Natural History. A new exhibition at the New York museum will examine the life and history of the dinosaur era reptiles known as pterosaurs, which were the first back-boned animals to evolve powered flight. “Pterosaurs as their own unique group, they were the first animals with backbones to achieve true powered flapping flight, so that they’re really unique in that way. They also represent the largest animals we know of ever to have powered flight. Some of them have wing spans up to ten meters across, which is a huge, huge animal. But as their own group, they’re not related to birds, they’re not related to bats, they’re just a unique group of reptiles that are closely related to dinosaurs but aren’t dinosaurs. When they evolved, they were very diverse and they lived on every continent.” While the reptiles may have become extinct 66 million years ago, scientists believe that pterosaurs diversified into more than 150 species of different shapes and sizes across the planet. Difficult words: vertebrate (animal which has a backbone), reptile (cold-blooded animal), evolve (change their bodies over time to be able to fly), backbone (row of bones down the centre of your back), diverse (different), diversify (change). Source: www.itn.co.uk

Here is some news from the USA. A soldier fought in Iraq. He is not mentally OK. He is under a lot of stress . He does something bad at a military base in Texas. He drives to two buildings. He starts to shoot a gun. He kills three people. He injures sixteen people. People stop the soldier. He kills himself. This is not the first shooting at this base. There was a shooting in 2009. That shooting killed thirteen people. It injured thirty-two people. President Obama is worried about this event. Difficult words: mentally (with the mind), to be under a lot of stress (to be very unhappy), military base (place with soldiers), injure (have problems with the body). You can read the original story and watch the video in the Level 3 section.

An American soldier drove to two buildings and opened fire at a military base in Texas. He killed three people and injured at least sixteen. Military police stopped the soldier. He then shot himself in the head. The soldier fought in Iraq and he was suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder . The military base was also the site of another shooting in 2009. In that shooting, thirteen people died and thirty-two were injured. The latest shooting is the third one at a military base in the USA in around six months. President Obama called the shooting troubling . Difficult words: open fire (begin to shoot), post-traumatic stress disorder (when a person is under a lot of stress because of something bad that happened), troubling (worrying). You can read the original story and watch the video in the Level 3 section.

A U.S. soldier shot three people dead and injured at least 16 on Wednesday before he took his own life at the Fort Hood Army Base in Texas. The soldier, who was being treated for post-traumatic stress disorder after fighting in Iraq, drove to two buildings on the base and opened fire before he was stopped by military police. He then shot himself in the head. The incident lasted between 15 and 20 minutes. All the wounded and killed were military personnel . Fort Hood was also the site of another deadly shooting rampage in 2009 where 13 people were killed and 32 wounded. Wednesday’s shooting is the third incident at a military base in the US in around six months. President Obama has called the shooting troubling. “The folks there have sacrificed so much on behalf of our freedom. Many of the people there have been through multiple tours in Iraq and Afghanistan. They serve with valour , and they serve with distinction . When they’re at their home base, they need to feel safe.” Difficult words: wound (to injure), military personnel (people who work in military force), rampage (period of violent and uncontrollable behaviour by a person or people), folks (people), sacrifice ( to give up something to help someone), valour (great courage), distinction (excellence). Source: www.itn.co.uk

A security camera captures a crime. It happens in England. A criminal is behind a man. This man is disabled . He rides on a mobility scooter . The criminal tries to take the man’s bag. The bag gets around the man’s neck. He cannot breathe , but the criminal keeps pulling the bag. The disabled man falls on the ground. The criminal finally gets the bag. He runs away. The criminal is caught. He goes to prison. He goes to prison for 40 months. Difficult words: disabled (he cannot use a part of his body), mobility scooter (electrical moving chair for people who cannot move), breathe (get air). You can read the original story and watch the video in the Level 3 section.

A security camera captured a shocking crime. It shows a drunk criminal who tries to steal a bag from a disabled man on a mobility scooter. It happened in England. The criminal approached to the man from behind. He tried to snatch the bag, but the bag’s cord got caught around the victim ’s neck. The victim couldn’t breathe, but the criminal did not let go of the bag. The disabled 42 year-old man fell on the ground. The 23 year-old criminal finally got the bag and ran off. The criminal was later recognised by the victim. The criminal was jailed for 40 months. Difficult words: snatch (take quickly), cord (object like a rope), victim (somebody who is attacked). You can read the original story and watch the video in the Level 3 section.

These shocking images show the moment a drunk thug tried to steal a bag from a disabled man on a mobility scooter. CCTV footage released by police shows the moment the thug creeps up behind his victim and tries to snatch the bag from his back. The victim was hauled from his scooter and onto the ground, after the bag’s cord got stuck around his neck. Daniel Jones from Nuneaton approached the 42 year-old man when he saw him on a late night supermarket trip in Coventry. Despite the victim gasping for breath when the bag was caught around his neck, Jones refused to release his grip and dragged him off the scooter. The 23 year-old finally managed to untangle the bag’s cord and ran off. After claiming he couldn’t remember anything about the incident, he was picked out during an ID parade , and was later jailed for 40 months after admitting robbery. Difficult words: thug (criminal), creep up (to surprise somebody from behind), snatch (take quickly), haul (pull), grip (firm hold), untangle (separate something twisted), claim (say), ID parade (the victim recognised the criminal from other people). Source: www.itn.co.uk

Drug gangs in Mexico are using social media. They want to show off and fight each other. Back in 2024, a big gang breaks into two groups. Now, they are fighting for control. They use young online stars to make videos and bring in new people. But this is very dangerous. At least 19 creators die. Some creators talk about gang life only to get views. Others help hide dirty money in normal businesses. The police do not stop the killers. The danger keeps growing. Social media companies try to block bad accounts, but it is not enough to keep young people safe. Difficult words: show off (to show something proudly to make others like or support you), hide (to put something in a place where nobody can see it), danger (a situation when something bad may happen). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In Mexico, social media is a dangerous battleground for drug cartels. Since a big cartel split into fighting groups in 2024, criminal gangs use popular influencers for propaganda , showing off power, and attracting young members. At least 19 internet stars died after being linked to criminal organizations. Some influencers make videos about drug culture for clicks, while others are investigated for helping cartels clean illegal money through private businesses and shops. Police struggle to stop the violence, and very few murders are ever solved. Social media companies try to ban bad profiles, but cartels use hidden codes to break rules. As a result, young influencers are still in danger. Difficult words: battleground (a place where a fight or war takes place), cartel (a large group of criminals), propaganda (information used to make people believe a certain idea or group). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Ever since the Sinaloa Cartel split into rival groups in 2024, social media has turned into a dangerous battleground for Mexico’s drug wars. The competing factions regularly target popular content creators, and use them to show off power, post propaganda , and recruit young people. Local influencers who adopt narco culture for clicks often get caught in the middle and put themselves directly in the sights of rival gangs. On top of that, federal agents are looking into dozens of creators accused of helping cartels clean dirty money through online shops, brand deals, and live donations. This deadly connection has already cost the lives of at least 19 influencers across the country. Weak police work, a lack of real punishment, and slow moderation by tech platforms mean cartels can keep using young creators as easy tools for cash and influence online. Difficult words: faction (a small, organized group within a larger organization or political party), propaganda (information, ideas, or rumors deliberately spread to influence public opinion or promote a political cause), lack (not enough of something). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Canada and Europe want to work closer together. Many people in Canada prefer to buy things from Europe instead of the United States. Trade with the United States is changing. European leaders are talking about how to help each other more. They want to share energy, keep prices low, and help students study in different countries. Some big countries in Europe say that the rules are not ready for a special membership . But they still want to be strong friends. Working together helps both Canada and Europe stay safe, protect their businesses, and keep their people happy. Difficult words: share (to give a part of something to others, or to use something together), membership (when a country or person belongs to a group, club, or organization), protect (to keep someone or something safe). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Canada and the EU are working to build a much stronger partnership. Because of trade problems and rising costs with the United States, many Canadians prefer to buy goods from Europe and support local businesses. European leaders discussed giving Canada a special status , but some countries like Germany and France say the rules are not clear yet. Even without a formal title, Canada and the EU are already working closer together on important projects. They are sharing plans for defense , energy, clean technology, and student programs. Both sides believe that building strong relationships outside of North America will help protect their economy, keep energy supplies safe, and make their nations stronger for the future. Difficult words: status (the official position of a person, country, or organization), defense (protecting a country, building, or person against attack or harm), supply (an amount of something available to be used). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A summit in Montreal has highlighted a growing push to deepen political and economic ties between Canada and the EU. Motivated by trade disputes, geopolitical friction , and economic pressures from the United States, many Canadians are actively favoring European trade over American imports. While European Commission leadership proposed the idea of making Canada an associate member , major member states like France and Germany remain hesitant due to treaty limits and undefined legal terms. Despite these political hurdles, practical integration is already accelerating across some sectors. Canada has joined joint defense procurement programs and is exploring agreements covering energy, critical raw materials, and student exchanges. Both Canadian and European leaders view this closer partnership as essential for protecting national sovereignty, reducing dangerous dependencies on global superpowers, and securing critical supply chains in an increasingly unstable global economy. Difficult words: friction (disagreement, conflict, or tension between people or groups with different views), associate member (a member of an organization or group who has limited rights or status compared to full members), procurement (obtaining or buying goods and services, especially for a government or organization). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The EU has a new rule to save forests. The rule is starting on 30 December 2026. Companies which sell things like coffee, palm oil, and chocolate must prove that they do not cut down trees. But some big companies are still buying palm oil from places in Indonesia. People cut down forests illegally there. Some countries want Europe to stop or change the rule. These countries are, for example, the US and Indonesia. But the EU must follow the rules strictly . Indonesia is losing many trees to big fires and farming. People hope that this new rule will stop companies from harming trees and help keep the earth green and safe. Difficult words: prove (to show that something is true), illegally (against rules), strictly (exactly). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The EU will start using new anti-deforestation rules on 30 December 2026. Companies which sell products like palm oil, coffee, and chocolate must prove they don’t cut down trees to make them. But environmental groups in Indonesia found that big international brands may be breaking these rules. Well-known companies like PepsiCo and Unilever recently bought palm oil from plantations linked to illegal forest clearing. Some countries, including the US and Indonesia, asked the EU to make the rules easier for businesses. But environmental activists say Europe must stay strong and enforce the law. Indonesia lost many forests to farming and fires, so strict checks are needed to protect nature and stop global forest destruction. Difficult words: anti-deforestation (about preventing or stopping the clearing of forests), brand (a product made by a company under a particular name), enforce (to make sure that a rule is followed). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The EU’s anti-deforestation law faces an enforcement test ahead of its launch on 30 December 2026. Under the new rules, companies selling goods such as palm oil, coffee, and cocoa must prove their products are not linked to land cleared after 2020. However, recent investigations by Indonesian environmental organizations reveal that major international consumer brands risk breaching these regulations. Reports show that companies like PepsiCo, Unilever, and Ferrero have bought palm oil from Indonesian plantations accused of recent illegal deforestation. Despite heavy political pressure and lobbying from major exporting nations like the United States and Indonesia to delay or soften the legislation, environmental activists insist the EU must strictly enforce the rules. Indonesia has lost vast areas of forest to illegal logging and agricultural clearing, which increased its vulnerability to severe wildfires. Experts emphasize that strict enforcement by European authorities will be essential to hold global corporations accountable and halt worldwide forest destruction. Difficult words: enforcement (compelling compliance with a law), lobby (to influence a politician or public official on an issue), vulnerability (the possibility of being attacked, damaged, or harmed). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Famous actor Sir Patrick Stewart dies at age 86. Many people around the world are sad today. Stewart is famous for his big roles in Star Trek and X-Men movies. He also loves acting on stage in big theater shows. His close friends say that he is a kind man. He loves his work very much. People love listening to his deep voice and watching him act. He shows that you can do big action movies and also play in old story plays on stage. Fans will miss him, but they can still watch his great films. Difficult words: sad (unhappy), stage (an area in a theater where actors are), miss (to feel sad because someone or something is no longer somewhere). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Famous British actor Sir Patrick Stewart passed away at the age of 86. Many friends and fans are sharing kind words about his life and work. Actor Ian McKellen called him a deeply loved and respected friend. Stewart became famous around the world for his main roles in Star Trek and the X-Men movies, but he also loved playing in classical theater and performed in many famous Shakespeare plays in Britain. People who worked with him say he was a very talented, kind, and hardworking actor who made deep stories easy for everyone to enjoy. Fans will always remember his great voice, his classic movies, and his famous theater roles. Difficult words: classical theater (traditional plays and dramatic art), perform (to act, sing, dance, or play music in front of people). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Tributes have poured in from around the world following the death of renowned British actor Sir Patrick Stewart at the age of 86. His close friend and co-star Sir Ian McKellen praised him as one of the most respected actors of his generation. Stewart built a legendary career that seamlessly bridged classical Shakespearean theater and massive Hollywood blockbusters. Although he earned international fame playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men , he always remained deeply connected to his stage roots at the Royal Shakespeare Company. Directors and fellow actors remembered him as a generous collaborator who brought immense humanity, discipline, and accessibility to every role he played, and his passing marks a huge loss for stage and screen. His final film performance will serve as a lasting farewell to fans worldwide. Difficult words: seamlessly (smoothly and continuously), collaborator (a person who works jointly with others on a project or activity), farewell (saying goodbye). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Many parents in Denmark are taking their kids out of big schools. Normal classrooms are too loud and hard for some children. A boy named Olav has autism . He only goes to school a few hours a week. He mostly learns outside on a farm with his family. Parents are starting local groups where kids can play, work with their hands, and feel safe without stress. Experts say that schools need to change because kids learn in different ways today. These groups help families stay happy and keep learning every day. Difficult words: loud (not quiet), autism (a change in a person’s brain which impacts thinking, speaking, and understanding the world), local (when something is in an area or neighborhood near you). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In Denmark, more and more parents are keeping their children home from traditional schools. Many neurodivergent children, like 12-year-old Olav, who has autism, find normal classrooms too loud and stressful. Because schools lack special resources, parents are creating alternative clubs. In these clubs, kids can learn outside by doing practical things, like working on organic farms or building boats, without feeling stressed. While government officials worry about test scores in reading and math, experts say the school system is old and needs big changes. Parents hope these new groups will give their kids a safe space to grow, feel happy again, and slowly return to learning. Difficult words: neurodivergent (thinking, learning, or behaving differently from most other people), lack (to not have enough of something, or to be completely without it), test score (a number or mark that shows how well a student did on an exam). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

More Danish parents are pulling their children out of mainstream schools. They argue that the traditional education system is far too rigid for neurodivergent kids. Children with autism or attention disorders, like 12-year-old Olav, often struggle with noisy classrooms and fixed daily schedules. Because public schools lack resources and specialized programs, many families have turned to alternative support systems, such as parent-led clubs. These spaces allow children to learn at their own pace through practical activities, like organic farming, while giving them a safe environment free from pressure. While politicians worry about falling academic standards in reading and math, educational researchers argue that the school system itself needs urgent reform rather than forcing children to fit into outdated models. These alternative clubs aim to rebuild confidence and help kids rebuild their relationship with learning. Difficult words: rigid (unable to be changed or adapted; strictly set), neurodivergent (having a brain that processes information differently than what is considered typical), academic standards (the levels of quality, knowledge, and achievement expected from students in school). Hackers attack emergency phone apps in Ukraine and Russia. People get scary fake messages on their phones about a nuclear attack , bad air, and street fights. Officials in Kyiv tell people not to worry. They say that the messages are fake. A short time later, people in Russia also get strange fake messages. Millions of people use these apps every day to stay safe. Experts say that hackers do this to scare people, make life hard, and stop people from trusting official safety news. It is a new way for both sides to fight online. Difficult words: nuclear attack (an attack by a nuclear rocket), strange (unusual, hard to understand), scare (to make someone worry or be afraid). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Both Ukraine and Russia say hackers attacked their official emergency apps with fake safety warnings. People in Ukraine got scary messages on their phones about radiation , chemical danger, and street fights. Officials told everyone it was a fake message from Russian hackers and said their air defense was completely safe. A few hours later, Russia said its own emergency app was also hacked, and people got messages in Ukrainian. Millions of people use these mobile apps every day to stay safe from real attacks. Experts say these digital attacks are meant to scare people, create confusion , and make people lose trust in official warning systems on both sides of the war. Difficult words: radiation (dangerous energy from a nuclear bomb or other objects), air defense (rockets and systems which shoot down planes, rockets, or drones), confusion (a situation in which people are uncertain or don’t understand what is happening). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Both Ukraine and Russia recently reported that their official emergency alert apps were hit by major cyberattacks, which triggered mass panic through fake notifications. In Kyiv, citizens received terrifying false warnings about nuclear radiation, chemical threats, and active street fighting, and they were told to stay inside. Ukrainian officials quickly blamed Russian hackers and reassured the public that the actual air defense systems were never compromised . Just hours later, Russia’s Ministry of Emergency Situations reported a similar cyberattack on its own app, which sent out fake alerts with Ukrainian phrasing and offensive language. These attacks target popular mobile apps that millions rely on daily as a backup to air raid sirens . Experts point out that both countries have advanced hacking teams, and digital sabotage is a key weapon for wearing down morale , creating chaos, and making ordinary people doubt official safety warnings on both sides of the war. Difficult words: compromised (weakened, damaged, or made vulnerable to unauthorized access or security failure), air raid siren (a loud device used to warn the public of an incoming air attack or missile threat), sabotage (destroying or damaging something on purpose to stop it from working), morale (the confidence, enthusiasm, and discipline of a person or group at a particular time). Image Source: Magnific A student moving from India to a smaller Canadian city may look forward to finding a few favourite places around campus. As the city will be home during term, a campus tour can help them picture where they would spend their time between classes. They can look for nearby outdoor space or ask about a college community and regular activities they could join. 1. Queen’s University At Queen’s University in Kingston, Campus Life provides information on student clubs, intramurals, recreational activities and volunteering in the city. Students can find activities on campus and ways to meet local people beyond it. The university has broad undergraduate and graduate choices. Applicants still need to choose the level and degree they want and meet its admission requirements. Queen’s offers incoming international first-year undergraduates early move-in access and dedicated academic and career advising. A recurring activity can give students somewhere to return after orientation. Student Academic Success Services provides writing and learning-strategy support. Students can discuss unfamiliar academic expectations there as assignments begin to require more independent work. Students considering residence should check the conditions in their offer. Residence has Living Learning Communities and interest-based options, but a bed-space commitment does not promise a particular room or building. Those conditions belong alongside the decision to study in Kingston. 2. The University of Guelph The campus is in Guelph in southwestern Ontario, with organized activities and nearby outdoor space students can use during the week. The Arboretum connects to campus through trails and forest. Outdoor space is another part of the setting to consider alongside the city’s size. At the University of Guelph , GryphLife brings together clubs, events, workshops and co-curricular opportunities. Student Volunteer Connections helps students find community volunteering that suits their interests and availability. A regular activity offers contact with people beyond orientation. International applicants from India can contact an in-country representative with admissions questions. Global Pre-Arrival Support advisors help new students with registration, housing and arrival matters. GO Transit serves the campus and provides a connection with the Toronto region. Students considering visits or commuting can check the current timetable from the intended starting point. 3. Brushing your teeth every day keeps your mouth healthy. If you stop cleaning your mouth, bad bacteria grow very fast. In a few days, your gums start to bleed and hurt. After a month, the bugs make holes in your teeth. We call these holes cavities. If you go a full year without brushing, your teeth can fall out. Also, the bacteria can get into your blood and make your heart, brain, and body sick. Brushing two times a day keeps your mouth clean, saves your teeth, and helps your body stay strong and happy. Difficult words: bacteria (small living organisms), gum (the pink flesh from where teeth grow), bleed (to lose blood, the red liquid in your body). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Your mouth needs daily cleaning to stay healthy. If you stop brushing and flossing , bad bacteria grow very fast. In just a few days, sticky plaque covers your teeth, and your gums bleed and swell. This early stage is called gingivitis. After a month, the bacteria break down tooth enamel and form cavities . If you ignore your teeth for a year, the infection gets much worse. Your gums pull away, the bone holding your teeth shrinks, and your teeth can fall out. Even worse, bad bacteria can get into your blood and cause serious health problems in your heart, kidneys, and brain. Brushing twice a day stops these dangerous bugs and protects your whole body. Difficult words: floss (to use a soft thread to clean between the teeth), plaque (a sticky film of bacteria on teeth), enamel (the top layer of a tooth), cavity (a hole in a tooth). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

If you stop oral hygiene , the balance between helpful bacteria and harmful pathobionts in your mouth quickly breaks down. Within just a few days, harmful bacteria multiply and create a sticky layer called dental plaque. This plaque irritates your gums, which can cause bleeding and inflammation , an early stage of disease called gingivitis. Within a month, the bacteria produce strong acids that eat away at tooth enamel and create painful cavities. If left untreated for several months, gingivitis worsens into periodontitis, which damages soft gum tissue and causes gums to pull away from your teeth. After a year without cleaning, chronic infection destroys the underlying bone and causes teeth to wobble and fall out. Even worse, damaged gums allow harmful bacteria to enter your bloodstream. From there, these microbes can travel through the body and worsen serious health conditions, including heart disease, diabetes, and memory disorders like Alzheimer’s. Difficult words: oral hygiene (keeping your mouth clean and free of disease by regular brushing and flossing), pathobiont (a potentially disease-causing microorganism that normally lives harmlessly in the body unless the balance is disrupted), inflammation (when part of the body becomes red, swollen, hot, and often painful as a reaction to injury or infection), enamel (the hard, shiny outer surface layer of a tooth). Hospital computers in Singapore stop working for almost ten hours on October 13. An IT company makes a mistake. They do not update the safety software on time. This makes it hard for people to get medicine, pay bills , or book visits. About 4,000 people must change their doctor visits to another day. But officials say that nobody is hurt and personal data is safe too. Doctors and nurses work by hand on paper to keep helping sick people. Leaders say sorry for the mistake. They are fixing the computers so this does not happen again. Difficult words: update (to make something more modern or install new software), bill (a document which shows how much money you must pay), fix (to repair something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

On October 13, Singapore’s public hospitals faced a nine-and-a-half-hour computer system failure . It happened because a tech company hired to update security rules didn’t do the work on time. The outage affected major services, including booking appointments, giving out medicine, and paying bills. About 4,000 patient visits had to be moved to other days, but no patients were hurt. Health leaders said the problem was not a cyberattack, and no private medical data was stolen. Doctors and nurses quickly used paper rules and manual backups to keep taking care of patients. The health agency is now checking the contractor’s work and fixing the system so that future technical mistakes don’t cause problems again. Difficult words: failure (a situation in which a system stops working correctly), outage (a period of time when a service, power supply, or computer system is not working), private (belonging to a specific person or group, not public). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A nine-and-a-half-hour IT outage that disrupted Singapore’s public healthcare clusters on October 13 was caused by a preventable error by an IT contractor. Senior Minister of State for Health told Parliament that the service provider failed to complete a required security update to the system. The disruption affected appointment bookings, medication dispensing , and billing across three major healthcare clusters. About 4,000 outpatient appointments had to be rescheduled. Although backup data centers were in place, both relied on the same shared system, which prevented an immediate recovery. Health officials confirmed that the incident was not a cyberattack and no patient data was compromised or lost. Healthcare workers successfully switched to manual procedures and ensured no patient safety incidents occurred. Difficult words: preventable (able to be stopped, avoided, or prevented before it happens), dispense (to prepare and give out medicine, goods, or services to people), compromised (weakened, damaged, or made vulnerable to security risks or failure). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Many planes in Europe get fake bomb warnings on Friday. The day before, 25 other flights get similar warnings. One plane from Rome to Lisbon has a bomb warning, but it lands safely . Police check the plane and find nothing. Four more planes get fake warnings. They fly from France. They land safely. Another plane going from Prague to Rome must land in Venice. Police in Europe are looking for the people who make these phone calls. All planes are safe, but officers are still checking everything to keep people safe when they fly. Difficult words: bomb warning (a message or call warning that a bomb is somewhere), flight (a journey by plane), safely (in a way which is not risky or harmful). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A series of fake bomb threats disrupted many flights across Europe on Friday. This happened after more than 25 flights faced similar threats on Thursday. One Ryanair plane flying from Rome to Lisbon got a warning about a bomb on board. The plane landed safely in Portugal, where police began searching the aircraft. In France, officials reported four more bomb warnings for planes in their airspace. Another flight from Prague to Rome had to land in Venice because of a safety warning. Thankfully , all planes landed safely, and emergency teams checked them carefully. European police are now investigating who is making these phone calls, but officials don’t know yet if the events are connected. Difficult words: series (several similar events, things, or people which come one after another), bomb threat (a message or call warning that a bomb is placed somewhere), thankfully (luckily). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A wave of anonymous bomb threats continued to disrupt European aviation on Friday, following at least 25 reported scares across the continent the previous day. Control towers placed a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon under high security alert after they received a call warning of an explosive device on board. The aircraft landed safely in Portugal, where security forces immediately launched thorough inspections. Simultaneously , French authorities confirmed four additional bomb alerts involving planes flying over their airspace, all of which landed safely for emergency checks. Elsewhere, a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome was diverted to Venice because of a similar security threat. European law enforcement agencies and judicial police have opened extensive investigations to identify the source of these widespread disruptions. While security teams have found no explosives so far, EU officials stated it remains too early to determine if the coordinated scares are linked. Difficult words: anonymous (made or done by someone whose name is not known or made public), simultaneously (happening, existing, or done at the same time), judicial police (branch of law enforcement responsible for criminal investigations and gathering evidence for legal proceedings). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A sad event happens in Spanish football. A 30-year-old player named Jesús de Miguel dies after a big game accident. He hits another player hard during a match. He hits his head and chest . Doctors take De Miguel to the hospital quickly. At first, he is not well, but he is stable . But everything changes in the night. On Tuesday morning, his football team says that De Miguel dies. Many players and fans are very sad. Officials stop some matches to remember him and help his sad family. Difficult words: chest (a person’s body between the neck and the stomach), hospital (a building where doctors and nurses look after sick people), stable (when something does not change). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Spanish football is in mourning after Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel died at age 30. During a second-division match against FC Andorra, he suffered head and chest injuries in a bad collision with the goalkeeper. De Miguel collapsed on the field and was rushed to the hospital by paramedics, who had to help him after his heart stopped in the ambulance. On Monday, doctors said his condition was serious but stable, and family members came to visit him. But his health got much worse during the night, and his club confirmed his death on Tuesday morning. Everyone at the club is heartbroken, and officials postponed some football matches to show respect for his family and friends. Difficult words: mourning (deep sadness when someone dies), collision (moving object or person striking violently against another), condition (how a person feels and well they are). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Tragedy has struck Spanish football following the death of Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel at the age of 30. The forward suffered severe head and chest injuries during a heavy collision with FC Andorra’s goalkeeper, who was sent off for the challenge. De Miguel collapsed on the pitch and received emergency treatment while visibly shaken players and fans looked on. Reports indicate he suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance on the way to the hospital, where paramedics managed to resuscitate him. Although his condition was initially reported as stable but serious on Monday, his health rapidly deteriorated overnight. Tenerife officially announced his tragic passing early Tuesday morning. The Spanish Football Federation has postponed scheduled Spanish Cup fixtures as the entire football community mourns the loss of the respected player, while authorities begin further investigations into the exact cause of death. Difficult words: cardiac arrest (a sudden loss of heart function, breathing, and consciousness), deteriorate (to become progressively worse in health, quality, or condition), fixture (a sports match or event that has been arranged to take place on a specific date). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A London court says that famous British actor Russell Brand is guilty of big crimes. He hurts four women and must now go to prison for a long time. Police say that more women will likely come and tell their stories now. The police say that it is good that women can speak. People will believe them now. The British prime minister thanks the women who tell the truth about Brand’s bad actions. Police are still looking into other stories about him. Brand will find out his time in prison soon. Difficult words: guilty (when someone is responsible for something bad they do), likely (when something may happen or be true), prime minister (the leader of a government). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

British comedian Russell Brand was found guilty of rape and sexual attack in a London court. Following the verdict, police leaders say they expect more victims to come forward with new claims. One of them explained that seeing a famous person held responsible gives other victims confidence to speak up. Brand, a former Hollywood actor once married to singer Katy Perry, now faces a long time in prison. British Prime Minister thanked the brave women who spoke out about his terrible crimes. Police are already looking into other complaints against Brand, including one from a girl who was 16 years old at the time. The 51-year-old former star will go to court for his formal sentencing . Difficult words: rape (the crime of forcing another person to have sex without their consent), victim (a person harmed, injured, or killed as a result of a crime, accident, or other event), sentencing (the official proceeding where a judge gives a verdict). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Following the high-profile conviction of British comedian and actor Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault, UK police chiefs expect more victims to step forward. London’s Metropolitan Police Commissioner stated that successful court verdicts often give additional survivors the confidence to report past abuse, knowing they will be believed. Brand, who previously starred in Hollywood films and was once married to pop singer Katy Perry, faces a lengthy prison sentence after a London court found him guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. He also faces ongoing investigations regarding additional allegations , including one involving a 16-year-old girl at the time of the incident. British Prime Minister praised the victims for their courage in bringing the horrific crimes to light. As one of Britain’s most prominent public figures convicted of sex offenses in recent years, Brand remains in custody and is awaiting his formal sentencing hearing. Difficult words: conviction (a formal declaration by a court of law that someone is guilty of a criminal offense), allegation (a claim that someone has done something illegal or wrong, typically one made without immediate proof), courage (the ability to do something frightening or difficult without showing fear). Tech companies want to put robots with AI into our homes. Meta makes a new robot called Max. It walks on two legs. Some people think robots which look like humans can help us clean, pick up things, and work. But other people say that robots make too many mistakes . They can break glass, fall, or get lost in small rooms. Also, home robots use cameras to see everything. This can make people feel unsafe in their own homes. Scientists are teaching robots how to walk safely with the help of 3D maps. But it will take a long time before robots can safely live with us. Difficult words: human (a person), mistake (an action with a bad end), get lost (when you cannot find your way). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Big tech companies are building humanoid robots to bring AI into our daily lives. Meta recently created a prototype robot called Max, and they hope it can work in homes and offices. Supporters say robots shaped like humans can move around rooms and use everyday tools easily. But tech critics argue that these robots are not ready for normal homes. Rooms have many small obstacles , and robots can easily break objects or fall over. To work well, these machines also need to record video of private rooms, which creates serious security and privacy risks. Researchers are using 3D maps to teach robots how to move safely, but experts still disagree on whether home robots will become part of real life anytime soon. Difficult words: humanoid (looking like a human), prototype (an early version of a machine or device), obstacle (an object or thing which blocks the way). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Big technology companies are investing heavily in humanoid robotics, and racing to bring AI from screen interfaces into physical homes and workplaces. Meta recently developed a prototype humanoid named Max in just three months. They want to provide a physical body for its digital AI assistant. Proponents argue that building robots with human-like form allows them to navigate spaces, handle tools, and use infrastructure designed specifically for people. However, tech critics argue that current AI remains unreliable for real-world physical tasks. Human environments present unpredictable challenges and make delicate interactions such as handling fragile household objects extremely difficult to execute safely. Furthermore, developing autonomous home assistants requires gathering vast amounts of spatial data. This raises major cybersecurity concerns regarding surveillance, data privacy, and potential hacking risks. While researchers work on advanced 3D spatial mapping to help machines navigate rooms, experts remain divided over whether consumer humanoid robots are an inevitable step forward or an overhyped financial gamble. Difficult words: prototype (an early model or sample built to test a concept, design, or process before mass production), proponent (a person who advocates or speaks in favor of an idea, proposal, or project), spatial (relating to physical space).
